planting.note: Direct sow or plant divisions in spring into saturated to shallowly flooded, acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; hairy umbrella-sedge grows naturally in wet meadows, marsh edges, and ditches across the eastern and southeastern US.

directions: Direct sow or plant divisions into saturated to shallowly flooded, acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade. Hairy umbrella-sedge takes its common name from the soft, hairy sheaths clasping its stems and from the loose, umbrella-like clusters of small brownish flower spikelets held above the grass-like foliage in summer. It grows naturally in wet meadows, marsh margins, roadside ditches, and pond edges across the eastern and southeastern United States, tolerating both consistently saturated soil and brief shallow flooding. In a home rain garden or pond margin it adds fine, upright texture and a long season of subtle bloom, requiring little care beyond consistent moisture once established. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor and control spread.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in shallow standing water or saturated soil in full sun to partial shade; three-way sedge is the only living species in its genus and grows naturally along pond and lake margins across nearly all of North America.

directions: Plant divisions in shallow standing water (up to a few inches deep) or saturated soil in full sun to partial shade. Three-way sedge is an unmistakable native wetland plant, its jointed, hollow, upright stems and neat three-ranked leaves giving it a distinctly bamboo-like appearance unlike any other native sedge, an effect enhanced by small brownish flower spikelets that dangle along the upper stem in summer. It grows along the shallow margins of ponds, lakes, and slow streams across nearly the entire United States and southern Canada, spreading by rhizome to form an attractive colony that provides cover for waterfowl and other wetland wildlife. In a home pond or rain garden it makes a striking vertical accent at the water's edge, tolerating both standing water and saturated soil, and it can be divided in spring to control spread or to start new plantings elsewhere.

planting.note: Direct sow or plant divisions in spring into moist to seasonally wet, acidic, low-fertility soil in full sun to partial shade; tall nutrush grows naturally in wet meadows, pine savannas, and prairie swales across the eastern and southeastern US.

directions: Direct sow or plant divisions into moist to seasonally wet, acidic, low-fertility soil in full sun to partial shade. Tall nutrush is a slender, upright wetland sedge easily identified by its small but strikingly hard, shiny, pearly-white to gray seeds, which persist decoratively into fall and are readily eaten by songbirds and small mammals. It grows naturally in wet meadows, prairie swales, and open pine savannas across the eastern and southeastern United States, adding fine, grass-like texture and subtle late-season interest to a native wet meadow or rain garden planting. It tolerates a range of moisture from consistently damp to briefly saturated soil and needs little care beyond occasional division of congested clumps to keep the planting vigorous.

planting.note: Direct sow or plant divisions in spring into saturated to shallowly flooded, acidic, nutrient-poor soil in full sun; Tracy's beaksedge grows naturally in the wet pine flatwoods, marshes, and roadside ditches of Florida and the Gulf Coastal Plain alongside pitcher plants and other bog natives.

directions: Direct sow or plant divisions into saturated to shallowly flooded, acidic, nutrient-poor soil in full sun. Tracy's beaksedge is a tall, wiry native beaksedge of Florida and the Gulf Coastal Plain, forming dense stands topped by clusters of small, dark beaked spikelets that add fine vertical texture to a wet meadow, marsh margin, or bog garden planting. It grows in the same wet, acidic, nutrient-poor flatwoods and marsh habitat as pitcher plants and orchids, making it a suitable low-maintenance companion for a Gulf Coast bog garden or naturalistic pond margin. It tolerates both consistently saturated soil and brief shallow flooding, spreading gradually by rhizome, and needs no fertilizer or soil amendment, since rich garden soil favors weeds over this specialized wetland native.
